Reflecting on how my role, responsibilities, and involvement across the business have developed over the past few months.

Building on the Foundations

In my last post, I broke down my role by process: how an idea becomes a product, how bundles are developed, launched, and refined, and how different parts of the business fit together behind the scenes.

Six months later, the day-to-day responsibilities remain largely the same. The difference is the level of ownership they now involve.

Rather than simply learning systems and supporting projects, I’ve increasingly been taking the lead. Whether that’s developing new bundle concepts, influencing merchandising decisions, managing supplier relationships, protecting margins across key product ranges, or helping define systems that haven’t been built yet, my role hasn’t changed direction so much as it has developed in depth.

The foundations remain the same, but the decisions, opportunities, and responsibilities built on top of them have grown considerably.

Bundles

One of the clearest examples of this development is the Mechanic’s Apprentice Tool Chest Kit.

At face value, it’s another product listing on the website. Behind the scenes, however, it brings together the full bundle development process. I identified the opportunity, defined the proposition, built the bundle structure, handled the commercial considerations, created the product, and managed its merchandising on the website.

What makes it particularly satisfying is that the proposition works from both perspectives. It provides genuine value to customers entering the trade while delivering strong margins for the business.

In its first few weeks, the kit generated approximately £15,000 in revenue, which provided encouraging evidence that the concept and its execution were working as intended.

The product also attracted attention internally, with the CEO highlighting it as a strong example of what SGS does well. The Graphic Design team subsequently featured it in a Product Listing Page advert, as it showcased the breadth of our product offering while presenting a strong opportunity to cross-sell complementary products across the website.

Maybe cut this final paragraph

The project is a good example of the type of work I enjoy most: identifying opportunities, developing commercially viable propositions, and taking ownership of their execution from concept through to launch. While the positive internal recognition was gratifying, the strongest measure of success has been the product’s early commercial performance, which validated the original opportunity and encouraged me to continue pursuing similar commercial initiatives.

Merchandising

One aspect of the role that has changed significantly is how I think about products on the website.

When I started, much of my focus was on the fundamentals: ensuring products were categorised correctly, had accurate titles and descriptions, and appeared in the right places on the site. While those responsibilities remain important, I now spend much more time considering how customers discover products and navigate a range.

Through working on category structures, merchandising, SEO, bundle creation and product positioning, I’ve developed a broader understanding of the customer journey. Rather than focusing solely on whether a product is visible, I now consider how customers are likely to find it, what information they need to make a decision, and how the surrounding products can help guide them towards the right solution.

One example was our Modular Storage range, where I used customer browsing behaviour and product performance data to guide merchandising decisions. This led to changes in category layouts and pinned product positions.

This shift has given me greater influence over how ranges are presented across the website. Instead of simply maintaining product listings, I am increasingly involved in shaping how products are structured, prioritised and surfaced to customers, using both performance data and customer behaviour to inform those decisions.

I have found this aspect of the role particularly interesting, as it sits at the intersection of customer behaviour, product strategy and ecommerce performance. As my understanding of these areas has developed, so too has the scope of my involvement in them. It is an area I expect to continue developing further, both as my responsibilities grow and as I gain a deeper understanding of how customers interact with the website.

Range Ownership

Another significant development has been moving beyond individual products and taking greater responsibility for entire ranges.

This has involved different types of decision-making, from selecting products and working with suppliers to developing categories and protecting profitability across established product lines.

Tetrosyl

One example was a recent expansion of our Tetrosyl range.

Compared with some of our larger categories, Tetrosyl represents a relatively small part of the business and has historically delivered modest margins. Despite this, I was given ownership of the range and responsibility for determining its future direction.

Rather than working to a predefined plan, I was responsible for evaluating the opportunity, identifying gaps within the portfolio, deciding which products should be introduced, and building the range proposal. This involved engaging directly with suppliers, discussing pricing and availability, assessing commercial viability, and recommending stock quantities ahead of launch.

Once the proposal had been developed, I presented my recommendations for approval before moving forward with implementation.

While the project was relatively small in scale, it represented an important step in my development. It was an opportunity to take ownership of a category, make commercially focused decisions, and influence what products SGS ultimately brought to market.

More than anything, it demonstrated how my role has evolved from maintaining product information to taking a more active role in shaping the product ranges themselves.

Socketry

The introduction of our Socketry range followed a slightly different path.

Unlike Tetrosyl, where I was given responsibility for developing an existing category, Socketry had already been ordered before my involvement. However, as the expected delivery date approached, much of the work required to prepare the range for launch was still outstanding.

I was initially asked to explore bundle opportunities within the range, but that quickly led to a much deeper involvement. Through building the bundles, I became familiar with the products, the incoming order and the expected delivery timeline. As a result, I often found myself acting as the main point of reference for updates, with managers regularly asking me about arrival dates, order contents and launch preparations.

While the products technically existed within our systems, much of the information needed to launch them properly had yet to be completed. I gathered additional product information, sourced dimensions, completed product listings and ensured the supporting data was in place. I also worked closely with the Graphic Design team, providing reference material and product information to help create imagery that accurately represented the contents of the various socket and foam insert sets.

Alongside this, I continued developing bundles and worked with the Ecommerce team to ensure the range was positioned effectively ahead of launch.

What made the project particularly interesting was that I became involved long before the products arrived in the warehouse. By the time the first stock arrived, much of the groundwork had already been completed, allowing the range to go live quickly and with a far stronger foundation than it otherwise would have had. Looking back, it was probably the first time I had been involved so extensively in a product range before a single item had even been sold.

Tool Chest Pricing

Alongside the Head of Buying, I was heavily involved in a comprehensive review of our Tool Chest range.

[Add pricing spreadsheet image here]

This is one of SGS’s most commercially important product categories, making even relatively small pricing decisions significant. Rising supplier costs, increasing import expenses and changing market conditions meant that much of the existing pricing structure needed revisiting.

Rather than reviewing products individually, we assessed the range as a whole. A tool chest cannot simply be priced according to its cost and target margin. Its position within the range also needs consideration. Moving one product can create issues elsewhere, narrowing the gap between ranges, undermining premium propositions or creating inconsistencies in the customer offering.

As a result, a significant amount of work went into understanding how individual products related to one another. We reviewed pricing hierarchies across the entire range, considered stockholding levels, assessed the effect of supplier cost increases and examined how future purchasing costs could impact margins. Decisions were often interconnected, with adjustments to one product requiring further changes elsewhere in order to maintain a logical structure.

What I found particularly interesting was the degree to which pricing became a strategic exercise rather than a mathematical one. The challenge was rarely calculating a new selling price. It was understanding the wider consequences of that change and ensuring the overall range remained commercially coherent.

It was one of the first projects where I was exposed to the commercial management of a major category at this level. While customers ultimately only see the final selling price, the process behind it involved detailed analysis and a considerable amount of discussion around the long-term direction of the range.

Shaping the Future: The New PIM

The most significant project I’m involved in at the moment isn’t live yet.

SGS is currently transitioning to a new Product Information Management (PIM) system and, alongside Emilia, I’m helping lead the business’ involvement in its development.

Rather than waiting for a finished product, we’re actively involved throughout the process. This includes reviewing new functionality, identifying gaps, testing features within the development environment, challenging proposed processes, and ensuring the platform supports the way SGS actually works.

My experience across bundles, product data, merchandising and range development has been particularly useful here. Having worked with the current systems on a daily basis, I’m able to identify where processes can be improved and where potential issues might emerge before the platform goes live.

What makes the project different from the others is that its impact won’t be tied to a single product, category or commercial result. The decisions being made now will influence how product information is managed across the business for years to come.

In many ways, it represents the clearest example of how my role has evolved. Half a year ago I was learning how to navigate our existing systems. Today, I’m helping define the requirements of the system that will eventually replace them.

The Engine Room

Alongside these larger projects sits the day-to-day work that doesn’t naturally earn its own section.

New products still need setting up. Categories need maintaining. Prices change. Attributes need refining. Product pages need reviewing and performance needs monitoring.

It’s not always the most visible work, but it’s where much of my time is spent, and it’s the foundation that everything else relies upon. The bundles, range reviews and larger projects discussed throughout this post only work because the underlying product data and processes are maintained properly.

Looking back, what stands out most isn’t any individual project, but the variety of work I’ve been able to contribute to over the past few months. I’ve had opportunities to work on product launches, range development, pricing strategy, merchandising, supplier discussions and now the development of a completely new PIM system.

Each project has presented different challenges, but together they’ve given me a much broader understanding of how the business operates and how the different departments contribute to getting products in front of customers.

With Black Friday preparations already underway and the PIM project continuing to gather momentum, the focus now shifts to the next set of challenges. I’m finding myself involved not only in the day-to-day operation of the website, but also in projects that will influence how we work in the future. That’s a responsibility I’ve enjoyed taking on, and one I’m keen to continue developing as the business evolves.

item.title: Product Data Assistant
item.author: briggstitus123@gmail.com (Titus Briggs)
item.description:
My Role and What I Do

This is a look at what I actually do at SGS Engineering — how my role works and why I enjoy it as much as I do.

When I first joined SGS Engineering, everything moved fast. Within a month I’d already picked up the core workflows — product setup, price changes, attributes & facets, and the PIM. It was a steep learning curve, but the good kind: the kind where you feel yourself becoming useful, not just busy.

Since then, my role has grown into something much bigger and more defined. I now handle products end-to-end — from the initial idea to the moment a customer sees them on the website. I work across data, pricing, content, logistics, and commercial strategy.

But the clearest way to understand the breadth of my role is through the thing I’ve become known for internally: Bundles.

Bundles tie together every part of my work, and they go far beyond the typical “group of products” you see on a product page. Because of how bundles are structured in the PIM, I’m also responsible for some of the highest-value areas of SGS’s business — especially the Modular Workshop range, which represents a major share of company profit. Even though these units appear on the website as single products, their modular nature means they’re still treated internally as bundles, with all the complexity that comes with that.

Recently I’ve been building hundreds of new combinations to support upcoming launches — including new components like power-strip-integrated pegboards and other additions to the SWS ecosystem. This work isn’t just administrative; it shapes how customers discover, compare, and ultimately buy large workshop systems. It also ensures our internal structure, pricing hierarchy, and commercial logic stay tight as the range expands.

Spotting Opportunities

Every bundle starts long before it exists in the PIM. The real work begins in the data.

I analyse what’s selling, what isn’t, where customers expect added value, and where the range feels thin or inconsistent. This is part sales analysis, part pattern recognition, and part understanding how customers actually shop on the website.

I look for things like:

  • Gaps in the range — missing sizes, missing combinations, or modules that customers clearly want to pair together
  • High-performing products that would convert even better when bundled
  • Slow movers that become more attractive when paired with complementary items
  • Customer behaviour signals from Clarity and analytics showing where people hesitate, compare, or drop off
  • Inconsistencies in pricing or hierarchy that a bundle can simplify

Sometimes the insight comes from numbers — a spike in sales, a dip, or a pattern across similar SKUs. Other times it comes from the structure of the range itself: a product that feels “orphaned”, a module that should logically sit with others, or a gap that becomes obvious once you map the ecosystem.

It’s a mix of detective work and commercial instinct - and eventually a pattern emerges.

Here’s an example of the kind of dataset I work with when spotting opportunities

Composition & Validation

Once I’ve identified an opportunity, I build an initial version of the bundle — a working model that defines the components, the structure, and the logic behind how it should function. This gives me something tangible to test.

From here, composition and validation run in parallel. I move back and forth between the technical build and the commercial reality, refining both until the bundle is structurally sound, commercially viable, and strategically useful.

Shaping the Structure

I refine the component mix and configuration rules to ensure the bundle is:

  • Structurally coherent
  • Technically accurate
  • Easy to understand
  • Consistent within the wider range

This stage is iterative — I adjust, test, and re-balance until the bundle feels intuitive and purposeful.

Checking Commercial Viability

As the structure evolves, I test it against the commercial checkpoints:

  • Stock Levels - confirming availability
  • Expected Delivery - especially for new or low-stock-items
  • Cost Prices - confirming the margin foundations
  • Bundle Pricing - calculating the combined pricing based on components
  • Margin - checking both full-price and discounted scenarios
  • Seasonal/PROMO Priorities - aligning with trading plans and campaign windows

A bundle that looks good on paper may still be rejected if it cannibalises a hero product or creates confusion. Conversely, a tighter‑margin bundle may still be worth building if it serves a strategic purpose.

Here’s an example of one of the bundles I’m currently developing. Stock isn’t due until August, but having everything built early means we’re fully prepared when it lands — and it also gives a clear insight into how I approach the bundle‑building process from the ground up.

Cross-Team Review

Once the specification is stable, I present it either directly to my managers or in the bi‑weekly cross‑team meeting I run (Ecommerce, Buying, Line Managers, Sales, PIM). This is where the bundle is challenged from technical, operational, and commercial angles.

Only once everyone is aligned do I move into the system build.

Building the Bundles

Once I’ve been given the all-clear, I move into the PIM to build the bundle as a structured product. This is where the planning becomes reality — and accuracy matters more than anything else.

This stage is about execution, not decision‑making. Everything must be built correctly so the bundle behaves exactly as intended on the website.

This includes:

  • Taxonomy Alignment - ensuring the bundle sits in the correct category structure
  • Dimension & Weight - confirming accurate logistics data so delivery methods, surcharges, and shipping rules calculate correctly
  • Titles & Descriptions - clear, consistent, and SEO-aligned
  • Attributes Mapping - making sure technical data flows cleanly to the website
  • Component linking - connecting all SKUs that make up the bundle

This stage is meticulous. A single incorrect attribute or missing link can break facets, hide the product from filters, or cause stock discrepancies. For complex ranges like SWS, where a single unit can contain dozens of components, accuracy is everything.

I also enter the product into our accounting software. While it doesn’t hold the same level of detail as the PIM, it’s essential for stock management, internal reporting, and ensuring Buying can track active inventory.

Once the data is in place, I send the spreadsheet to Graphic Design — often including reference imagery — so they can create new assets. It may include callout graphics, lifestyle imagery etc. These assets are crucial for conversion. A bundle can be commercially perfect, but without strong imagery, it won’t perform.

The Web

This stage is where the technical build meets real-world customer behaviour — and small details can make a big difference to visibility and conversion.

I check that the bundle has pulled through correctly to the front end, ensuring:

  • Facets are mapped accurately
  • The product appears on the correct category page
  • It’s pinned or prioritised where relevant
  • I link similar or complementary products
  • I collaborate with Ecommerce to feature it in banners or promotional placement

This stage is about making sure the bundle is not only live but discoverable, logical, and positioned to convert.

Sometimes a product pulls through correctly, but the facets don’t surface it where customers expect. For example, I’ve had bundles appear on the category page but not show up when filtering by drawer count. After investigating, I found that one inherited attribute wasn’t mapped correctly from a component SKU. Fixing the mapping immediately improved visibility and traffic.

Tracking

After launch, I monitor performance and make continuous improvements. I use Microsoft Clarity and the built‑in web reports to understand how customers interact with the product page — where they scroll, what they click, how long they stay, and how they navigate to the listing.

I track:

  • Customer behaviour
  • Traffic sources
  • Conversion indicators
  • Early sales performance

This data helps me refine the product over time. Sometimes the improvements are small — adjusting image order, tightening a title, or improving the first paragraph of the description. Other times they’re structural.

For example, with the new SWS components, I noticed customers weren’t scrolling far enough to reach the product callout section. It was positioned too low on the page and wasn’t treated as a primary asset. I updated the layout so the callout became a main visual element — improving visibility, engagement, and overall clarity.

Tracking isn’t a one‑off task; it’s a feedback loop. Each insight feeds back into the product, the category, or even the wider range strategy. It’s how I make sure the bundles I build don’t just go live — they perform.

Summary

Although bundles aren’t the only part of my job — and I’m always juggling a wide range of tasks — they highlight every aspect of my role:

  • Data Analysis
  • Sales Insights
  • Pricing Logic
  • PIM expertise
  • Cross-team Collaboration
  • E-commerce Optimisation
  • Continuous Improvement

They’re the clearest example of how I take an idea, extract the data, structure it, build it, launch it, and then track and refine it. It’s the full lifecycle — and one of the parts of my role I’m most proud of.

I’ve genuinely landed well at SGS Engineering. I’m happy with the work I’m doing and the opportunities it offers. Sales are up, management is capable and enthusiastic, and meetings actually lead to decisions and progress. It’s an exciting environment to be part of, and I’m glad to be contributing to it.

What I enjoy most is that my work has a direct impact — on the website, on the customer journey, and on the commercial performance of the business. It’s a role that keeps growing with me, and I’m excited to see where it goes next.

item.title: Workflow
item.author: briggstitus123@gmail.com (Titus Briggs)
item.description:
I’ve taken the chance to reflect on the years I spent at Nottingham Trent University — and on the tools and systems that quietly shaped how I work today.

More than anything, I’ve realised that good systems don’t just help your work, they change the way you work.

Reflection

Graduating felt like closing a long chapter — one full of challenges, growth, deadlines, and a lot of learning that happened just as much outside the lecture theatre as inside it.

Looking back, one thing stands out more than anything else: the systems I built to stay organised, focused, and consistent.

They weren’t particularly glamorous. They didn’t make the work disappear, and they certainly didn’t stop deadlines from piling up. But they gave me something much more useful: a reliable way of dealing with the work when everything else felt chaotic.

That became increasingly important as university progressed. I was balancing full-time work alongside my degree, managing coursework and eventually a dissertation, while still trying to maintain some kind of life outside of all of it.

The tools I used became more than just productivity software. Over time, they changed how I approached problems.

Doom Emacs

The tool that probably had the biggest influence on how I work is Doom Emacs.

I won’t attempt a full technical breakdown — there are entire wikis dedicated to that — but the simplest way I can describe it is:

Doom Emacs is a fast, keyboard-driven, endlessly customisable environment built around structure and clarity.

I used it as a central hub for a few things that mattered most:

  • Planning deadlines and upcoming work
  • Managing tasks and projects
  • Writing structured notes and coursework

What surprised me wasn’t just how much I could do with it, but how much it changed the way I thought.

Org-mode encourages you to break large problems into smaller ones, outline ideas, and give information some structure before trying to act on it. Eventually, that stopped being something I did inside Emacs and became something I did almost automatically.

A typical day started in much the same way: open my agenda, look at what was coming up, review anything overdue, capture anything new, and start working.

That routine became particularly useful during dissertation season.

With deadlines approaching and a seemingly endless list of things to read, write, research, and fix, it was surprisingly easy to lose sight of what actually needed doing. Instead of keeping everything in my head, I could break the dissertation down into sections, tasks, sources, notes, and smaller pieces of work.

Rather than thinking “I need to finish my dissertation”, I could look at the next concrete thing that needed doing.

That distinction sounds small, but it made a huge difference.

The same approach carried over into revision and coursework. During lectures, I’d capture notes under structured headings. Later, those notes could become the starting point for revision or an assignment. The work wasn’t necessarily easier — but the process was much less chaotic.

There was also, admittedly, a downside.

Emacs makes it incredibly easy to optimise the system instead of actually using it.

I’d sit down intending to work and think, “I’ll just add this keybinding.” Then I’d realise that another package could make it slightly better. Then I’d need to configure that package. Then I’d discover something else I could customise.

An hour later, I’d have a beautifully configured productivity system and absolutely no additional work done.

I’ve definitely fallen into that trap more times than I’d like to admit.

But those hours weren’t entirely wasted. Learning how the system worked meant I could eventually shape it around the way I actually worked rather than constantly adapting myself to someone else’s workflow.

That lesson has stuck with me: there’s value in understanding the tools you depend on, but the tool should ultimately serve the work.

I still use Doom Emacs today — including to write this post — and I can’t see myself switching anytime soon.

Here’s today’s TO DO list, for example.

It’s not an especially exciting list, but it gives a good idea of how I use the system to turn a collection of things in my head into something concrete and manageable.

Syncthing

If Doom Emacs taught me how useful structure could be, Syncthing taught me the value of reliability.

My interest in it came from a much less organised place.

During my first year, I lost handwritten notes. Later, I ran into the usual problems with cloud storage and OneNote — files not being where I expected them, syncing issues, and the general frustration of relying on a service to keep everything available when I needed it.

I wanted something simpler.

I had an old desktop PC sitting around, alongside my laptop, and realised I could use Syncthing to keep the two in sync without handing control of my files over to another service.

The setup was straightforward: save a file on one machine and, shortly afterwards, it would appear on the other.

That might not sound particularly impressive, but during university it removed an entire category of things I had to worry about.

My files were available across my devices. Changes were synchronised automatically. I didn’t have to remember to manually copy everything across before leaving the house or worry that the only copy of an important document was sitting on one machine.

During dissertation season, that peace of mind mattered.

Syncthing didn’t make the dissertation any easier to write, but it made the environment around it more dependable.

And that’s something I’ve come to appreciate more generally: good systems often become invisible when they’re working properly.

The best outcome isn’t thinking about the system constantly. It’s forgetting that it exists because it’s quietly doing what it’s supposed to do.

What I Took From It

Looking back, the individual tools matter less to me than what using them taught me.

Doom Emacs taught me to break problems down.

Syncthing taught me to think about reliability and failure.

And spending years building my own workflows taught me to question processes that felt unnecessarily complicated.

There were plenty of times when I over-engineered things. I’ve spent hours configuring software when I probably should have been doing the work itself. But that experimentation also taught me how to recognise the difference between a useful system and one that exists purely because it was interesting to build.

More importantly, it changed the way I approach unfamiliar problems.

When something feels overwhelming, my instinct is now to break it down.

When something is repetitive, I look for a way to automate it.

When information is difficult to manage, I look for a better structure.

And when something keeps going wrong, I try to understand why rather than simply working around it.

That’s probably the biggest lesson I’ve taken from university.

Good systems don’t just help your work, they change the way you work.

Looking Ahead

As I move into my role as Product Data Assistant at SGS Engineering, I’m taking that mindset with me.

I don’t expect my university workflows to survive unchanged. In fact, I expect the opposite. Different problems will require different systems, and I’ll have to adapt to the tools, processes, and people around me.

But the underlying approach remains the same.

Building a website, maintaining a GitHub repository, refining my Emacs configuration, and designing my own workflows have all taught me to look at problems in terms of systems rather than isolated tasks.

If a system doesn’t exist, I can build one.

If a workflow is clunky, I can improve it.

If information is messy, I can structure it.

That’s the mindset I’m taking into the next chapter.

This site is becoming part portfolio, part blog, and I’m completely fine with that. If anything, it feels more honest. The things I build and the things I write about are both part of the same process: figuring out how I work, what I can improve, and what I want to learn next.

Thanks for reading. More to come.

item.title: Sport Performance Data Analytics
item.author: briggstitus123@gmail.com (Titus Briggs)
item.description:
Nottingham | Aug 2023 to May 2024

Nova Centurion Swimming Club

During my time at the club, I worked hands-on with 30+ elite swimmers, independently leading all aspects of performance analysis. I gathered and cleaned data from heart rate monitors, hydration tools, lap timing systems and other sources, translating it into practical insights for athletes and coaches.

By tracking time-series data and identifying longer-term performance trends, I supported coaches in shaping more targeted training sessions. I also designed visual dashboards and summary reports to aid evidence-based decisions. One of the most rewarding aspects was running collaborative goal-setting sessions — helping athletes translate technical metrics into realistic, actionable targets.

Outside of analysis, I liaised with external suppliers like 1080 Motion to explore new tools for performance enhancement. I also got stuck into club events, including swim meets, where I handled branding — from concept to print — producing sponsor-backed banners that still hang proudly at the pool today.

All data was handled securely, in full compliance with GDPR and safeguarding policies, and I regularly presented my findings to senior coaching staff as part of wider discussions on athlete progression and long-term development.

Reflections and Highlights

One memorable highlight was travelling with the team to Liverpool at the end of Cycle 2. That meet saw many swimmers hit personal bests — a real validation of the work we’d done together as a coaching and support team.

I’m particularly proud that eight swimmers qualified for the Olympic trials during my time at the club. It speaks volumes about the strength of the programme and the collaborative effort driving it forward — data, coaching, and athlete commitment all pulling in the same direction.

That experience solidified just how much I enjoy working at the intersection of performance data and human potential. It’s not just about crunching numbers — it’s about using insight to unlock growth, identify meaningful goals, and support people as they push beyond what they thought possible. Along the way, I found myself diving deeper into data visualisation, exploring the biomechanics of elite movement, and constantly thinking about how best to communicate technical insight to a broader audience.

Since leaving, I was delighted to see the club featured in a BBC News segment highlighting its impressive scholarship programme and close ties with Nottingham’s two universities. David — one of the swimmers I got to know well — was front and centre. Seeing their continued success reminds me how valuable that chapter was in shaping how I think about performance, people, and potential.

You can check out the post here on LinkedIn.

The Data

Pivotal to my role was the manual collection of lap times. I recorded finishes as swimmers hit the wall—scribbling times while mentally tracking who touched in which lane, often just seconds apart. The pace was relentless, and there was no margin for hesitation. It was a baptism of fire, but I quickly learned the importance of staying organised, thinking ahead, and keeping calm under pressure.

Between sets, while the athletes were swimming down, I transferred everything into spreadsheets (like the one pictured above). I’d calculate average split times for each set, along with sectional breakdowns where relevant, and compare them to previous sessions and cycle averages. Each week, I’d share the stats on a whiteboard so swimmers could track their progress visually — a small ritual that turned into a strong motivational anchor during tough training blocks.

When time allowed, I created dashboards to highlight trends and standout performances. But truthfully, fitting that in around a full-on schedule was a challenge. I arriving at the pool by 5:15 to set up for morning training before heading straight to my management job — then returning again for the evening session. It was relentless, and most days left little time for any rest.

What kept me going was the sheer dedication I saw in the swimmers — showing up day after day with focus, drive, and zero complaints. I had huge respect for their work ethic, and that motivated me to match their commitment in my own way. Even in the tougher moments, I wanted to make sure I was giving them the support they deserved.

Eventually, the inevitable caught up with me and I experienced burnout for the first time. It was a difficult chapter, but one that forced me to reassess how I worked. I learned to set firmer boundaries, prioritise more effectively, and find smarter, more sustainable ways to manage pressure — lessons I now carry with me into every project.

In hindsight, I would’ve loved more time to refine those dashboards consistently. But the dynamic, fast-paced nature of training meant flexibility was key, and the experience taught me more about resilience and adaptability than any spreadsheet ever could.

Technique Analysis

A core part of my role involved poolside video analysis, using GoPros and iPads to capture training sessions from multiple angles. We’d film specific sets or drills — often focusing on starts, turns, or pacing segments — so swimmers could immediately watch their technique and reflect on what needed adjusting.

This approach enabled instant, stroke-specific feedback. Whether it was sharpening a freestyle entry, maintaining streamline off the wall, or correcting a timing issue on breaststroke, the visual element gave swimmers a new level of understanding. Many of them were quick to engage with it — watching clips back between reps or discussing technique on the spot during recovery intervals.

Beyond technical gains, it helped strengthen relationships. The process created a two-way dialogue: swimmers became more confident analysing their own performances, and I learned how different athletes absorbed feedback best — some visually, others through analogy or focused key words.

Even without editing software or extended review time, the combination of accessible technology and real-time playback made a tangible impact in day-to-day training. For the athletes, it turned abstract corrections into visible cues. For me, it underscored just how powerful simple tools can be when used consistently and with purpose.

Heart Rate Tracking

Each session, swimmers wore Polar heart rate monitors clipped to their goggles. This allowed the head coach to implement zonal training — a highly effective approach that could be tailored to each athlete, whether they were sprinters, distance swimmers, or coming back from injury.

Swimmers were often keen to review their data after key sets, particularly their recovery rates and how hard they’d pushed within target zones. It became a meaningful way for them to reflect on their effort — and for us to ensure their training intensity matched individual capacity, not just the pace of the group.

This mattered especially in a squad with such varied profiles — different ages, genders, and stages of development all training side by side. Time is a useful metric, but it doesn’t always tell the full story. Heart rate data offered a more personalised lens into each swimmer’s physiological response, helping us coach with more nuance and care.

It was particularly valuable in cases where swimmers were returning from injury, or for our Para swimmer, who trained with remarkable consistency. Being able to monitor effort through zones helped keep sessions productive without tipping into overload.

In hindsight, I’d have loved to dig deeper into long-term patterns — comparing weekly zone distribution, recovery trajectories, and perhaps even linking heart rate data to taper outcomes. There’s huge potential in that kind of analysis, and it’s something I’d jump at exploring further.

Goal Setting

At the start of each cycle, I worked with swimmers to set both performance targets and technical goals — whether that meant hitting a new 100 m PB or refining their breakout from the wall. It wasn’t just about chasing time; we aimed to make their goals as specific, personal, and measurable as possible.

At every swim meet, I updated a central spreadsheet with their best times, calculating how close they were to their personal bests and target splits — both in percentages and raw seconds. While we gathered plenty of day-to-day training data, it was those meets that gave swimmers a clearer sense of progression. Being less frequent, they stood as proper milestones — moments to pause, reflect, and re-calibrate.

This process became a strong motivator. Swimmers would often check in to see how far off they were from a certain target or how they were trending across cycles. The visual feedback — especially when paired with consistent goal updates — helped them stay focused during long blocks of training.

We revisited and adjusted goals regularly, especially as technique improved or confidence grew. I found this aspect of the role particularly rewarding — especially early on, when I was still getting to know the squad. It gave me a real window into each athlete’s mindset, their ambitions, and the quiet drive that powered their progress in and out of the pool.

Hydration

Like clockwork, every Saturday before sunrise, I’d be poolside — clipboard in hand, collecting neatly labelled bottles from swimmers who were already stretching or warming up. Asking for urine samples at 5:30 am might sound awkward, but within the squad it was standard procedure — routine, professional, and completely normalised. The swimmers were used to it, and it was all handled without fuss or weirdness.

Hydration testing might not be the most glamorous aspect of performance support, but it was one of the most impactful. It’s often overlooked despite being one of the easiest variables to control — and it plays a huge role in recovery, output, and overall consistency in the water.

After testing, I gave each swimmer their individual results privately, with a quick explanation of where they stood. Over time, it became a bit of a friendly rivalry — athletes competing (quietly) to be the most consistent or to bounce back quickest after hard sessions. That unspoken competition actually helped me keep them engaged and proactive — they took ownership of it, which made the data far more meaningful.

It’s not the sort of work that makes the highlight reel, but it quietly underpinned a lot of the athletes’ day-to-day success — and reinforced how the smallest habits can create the biggest differences when practised consistently.
